lead: Cloud computing for IoT is a shared, elastic pool of computing, storage and services reached over a network. It exists because tiny sensor nodes cannot store years of readings or run heavy analytics. A sensor cloud goes further: many physical sensors appear as virtual sensors that applications can query. You meet it in smart meters, fleet tracking and city air-quality dashboards.
prereq: You need Unit 1 logical design and communication models, Unit 2 sensor nodes and Unit 3 MQTT publish-subscribe basics.

blocks.text: Cloud computing is a model for giving computing, storage and software as a service over a network. For IoT it solves a size problem: a sensor node may have kilobytes of RAM, while a city has years of readings. The cloud also adds servers when traffic rises and removes them when it falls.

items: On-demand self-service: a team requests a virtual machine or database through a portal and gets it without a human operator.
Broad network access: services are reached over standard networks, from phones, gateways or laptops.
Resource pooling: many customers share a pool of servers; the provider assigns and reassigns capacity.
Rapid elasticity: capacity grows or shrinks quickly with demand, often automatically.
Measured service: usage is metered, so you pay for what you consume.

blocks.text: A Chennai apartment using water meters shows the need. Two hundred meters send small readings. A cloud broker receives them, keeps months of history and runs billing. At the month end, billing jobs need more CPU; elasticity adds it. For the rest of the month, the system shrinks. Measured service turns this into a variable cost instead of a large server purchase.

Virtualization lets one physical computer run several isolated systems. The physical machine is the host. A hypervisor is software that creates and runs guest virtual machines (VMs). Each guest VM has its own virtual CPU, memory, disk and operating system. A VM image is a packaged disk and configuration from which a new VM starts. Provisioning creates the VM from an image. Templates repeat common settings. Snapshots save a point-in-time state before an upgrade. Monitoring watches CPU, memory, disk and network; scaling adds or removes instances.

Containers package an application with its libraries but share the host operating system kernel. A container image is the packaged filesystem and settings. A running container is an instance of that image. Namespaces isolate what a process can see, such as its process list and network. Control groups, or cgroups, limit and account for CPU, memory and I/O. Docker is a common packaging and runtime tool.

The difference matters for IoT. A VM is heavier: each guest carries a full OS. It gives strong isolation between different OS families. A container is lighter and starts faster, but it must match the host kernel family. A Linux container needs a Linux host kernel; it is not a small VM. Use VMs for hostile multi-tenant separation, containers for many small services.

sections.h3: Service models, deployment, IoT platforms and sensor clouds

blocks.text: Cloud services come in three standard models. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) gives virtual machines, storage and networks; you manage the operating system and runtime. PaaS (Platform as a Service) gives a runtime, database and scaling; you deploy code and the provider manages servers. SaaS (Software as a Service) gives a finished application, such as a dashboard, used through a browser.

Deployment models describe who shares the cloud. A public cloud is owned by a provider and open to many customers. A private cloud is used by one organisation, with self-service and pooling. A hybrid cloud joins public and private resources under common management. A community cloud is shared by organisations with a common concern, such as hospitals.

An IoT platform is a PaaS-like service for devices. Typical IoT cloud services are a device registry, a message broker, rules, time-series storage, alerts and dashboards. In a cloud IoT architecture, devices connect through gateways to the broker; streams go to storage and analytics; applications read results. Identity and device management give each device a credential, keys, permissions and a revocation path. This is not user login; a stolen meter credential must be disabled without affecting other meters.

A sensor cloud exposes physical sensors as virtual sensors. The broker ingests readings, keeps metadata and offers an API. A billing application asks a virtual sensor for a meter's history; it does not address the physical node. The figure shows this path.

figure.caption: Two hundred meters each send 48 readings a day; the broker ingests 9,600 readings (0.6144 MB) a day and holds 90 days of raw data — 55.296 MB — then hands each meter out as its own virtual sensor to billing and leak analytics. Notice the broker is where readings pile up, and the virtual sensors are what applications actually talk to.

spec.title: Water-meter sensor cloud
spec.aria: 200 water meters each send 48 readings a day through a gateway to a cloud broker that ingests 9,600 readings (0.6144 MB) a day and stores 55.296 MB over 90 days, then exposes one virtual sensor per meter to billing and leak analytics.

examples.question: An apartment water-meter cloud serves 200 meters. Each meter sends one 64-byte reading every 30 minutes. Find readings per day, raw data per day in bytes and MB, and raw data stored for 90 days in bytes and MB. Use 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes.
steps: Readings per meter per day: 24 hours = 24 × 60 = 1,440 minutes; 1,440 ÷ 30 = 48 readings.
examples.answer: The cloud handles 9,600 readings/day, 614,400 bytes/day = 0.6144 MB/day, and 55,296,000 bytes = 55.296 MB in 90 days.
examples.check:
meters = 200
bytes_per_reading = 64
readings_per_meter = 24 * 60 // 30
readings_per_day = meters * readings_per_meter
bytes_per_day = readings_per_day * bytes_per_reading
mb_per_day = bytes_per_day / 1_000_000
bytes_90 = bytes_per_day * 90
mb_90 = bytes_90 / 1_000_000
print(readings_per_day)
print(bytes_per_day)
print(mb_per_day)
print(bytes_90)
print(mb_90)

traps: A container is not a small VM; it shares the host kernel and needs the same OS family.
A sensor cloud is not just cloud storage; it exposes and manages virtual sensors.
Elasticity is not free unlimited capacity; measured service bills the resources you use.
Private cloud is not merely an on-premises server; self-service, pooling and automation are part of the definition.
Device identity is not user login; revoking one device must not break others.

quiz.q: Define rapid elasticity in cloud computing.
quiz.a: Rapid elasticity is the ability to add or remove computing capacity quickly as demand changes, often automatically.

quiz.q: Why is measured service useful for an IoT water-meter cloud?
quiz.a: It bills actual use, so the operator pays more during month-end billing jobs and less when traffic is low, instead of buying a large fixed server.

quiz.q: A cloud serves 500 meters. Each sends one 40-byte reading every 15 minutes. Find readings/day and raw MB/day. Use 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes.
quiz.a: Readings per meter/day = 1,440 ÷ 15 = 96. All meters = 500 × 96 = 48,000 readings/day. Bytes/day = 48,000 × 40 = 1,920,000 bytes/day = 1.92 MB/day.

quiz.q: A team wants 50 small protocol adapters on one host. Compare containers and VMs for startup, isolation and kernel choice.
quiz.a: Containers start faster and pack more adapters per host but share the host kernel and need the same OS family. VMs give full OS isolation and allow different OS families, but each VM carries an OS, uses more memory and boots slower.

quiz.q: When should an IoT team choose PaaS over IaaS?
quiz.a: Choose PaaS when the team wants to deploy device-handling code and data without managing servers, OS patches and scaling rules. Choose IaaS when it needs control of the OS, broker or network.

quiz.q: Name the four cloud deployment models.
quiz.a: Public, private, hybrid and community cloud.

quiz.q: Why is a sensor cloud more than cloud storage for sensor readings?
quiz.a: It gives each physical sensor a managed virtual presence with metadata, identity, access and an API. Applications query virtual sensors and history without knowing the physical node or its protocol.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, IoT clouds increasingly push some analytics to edge gateways to cut latency and bandwidth, then use the cloud for long-term storage and model training. Kubernetes-style container orchestration is common for broker and analytics services. Serverless functions handle sporadic device events. Digital twins keep a cloud model of each physical asset. Search for edge computing, fog computing, Kubernetes, serverless IoT and digital twin.
